# The average customer now saves 25% with SFC#

September 9, 2026

The average customer now saves 25%

Evan Conrad CEO

Today, on-platform customers on SFC receive an average 25% realized discount off their compute price, via resale.

That means a customer buying $100k of compute receives $25k back from selling idle capacity, on average. For a customer who bought at $4.50/GPU/hr, that brings their realized price to $3.375/GPU/hr.

## How to maximize your utilization#

To maximize your realized price per GPU hour, SFC implements an order book that lets you get reserved capacity and then sell that capacity later. This lets you safely buy larger quantities, increasing your revenue, without taking the catastrophic risk that other locked in, long term contracts allow.

For most customers, this process is automatic. If you don’t want your node, just turn it off.

However, this article shows how some folks maximally use SFC to maximize their utilization, snatch up very cheap compute, and reduce their overall risk. It walks through how we built givemeanode, our autoresearch product, on top of SFC as a market maker.

Givemeanode turns wholesale GPU capacity into nodes for customer work. Its capacity manager, called the treasury, buys time on SFC and sells time it does not need. It also places bids for future dates.

The examples below build up this process, one decision at a time. Each node has eight GPUs. The treasury limits each order to 24 hours, but delivery can be many days away. The six-month view above shows the broader planning idea.

...

A bid is an offer to buy. An ask is an offer to sell. Both specify a price and a delivery window.

The treasury reads prices for each eligible SKU. It selects the lowest ask within its buy limit. All candidates must meet the work's hardware needs.

In use Resold Bought Idle

$16 is the lowest ask · limit $18 / node-hour

Here, SKU B costs $16 per node-hour. It is cheaper than SKU A at $18. When prices change, SKU A becomes the next choice.

...

This buy order requests one node for 12 hours. Its $18 limit is per node-hour, or $2.25 per GPU-hour for this eight-GPU node. Its maximum cost is $216.

...

At a fill price of $8 per node-hour, the four-hour sale returns $32 before fees. The sell limit is a minimum price. Resale fees reduce the credit received. A listing earns nothing until it fills.

The treasury can lower an ask as unused time approaches. Its price schedule keeps track of earlier price reductions, so a replacement listing does not restart at the original high price.

For a short resale window, a price ramp can also stay just below the best ask.

...

The treasury also buys ahead of confirmed demand. It divides future time into 24-hour UTC blocks and sets an hourly budget for each block.

Near dates receive a larger budget than distant dates. A continuous day can receive a higher bid than a short remaining window. Lower bids use the rest of the budget to seek more nodes.

In use Resold Bought Idle

$16 / hour × 24 hours = $384 held

In this example, a $32 hourly budget supports one $16 bid and two $8 bids. All three could fill. The maximum credit hold for the day is $768.

results.title: Run agent-driven experiments with SF Autoresearch | SF Compute
results.author: San Francisco Compute
highlights:
## Scale through SFC’s order book#

Autoresearch buys compute through SFC’s order book, a physically settled market where customers buy and resell GPU capacity. SFC operates every cluster it sells capacity on. That gives you a path from one experiment to thousands of GPUs without a long-term capacity commitment. Scale independent experiments and batch jobs across the fleet as capacity becomes available.

SFC’s upcoming deployments will expand that supply. The same market connects Autoresearch to capacity from the new clusters coming online, so your experiments can grow with the fleet.

...

The queue favors customers with less compute already in use. Your first node gets priority ahead of paid queue tiers. That keeps room for experimentation while larger campaigns make progress. You can inspect your position while you wait; priority doesn’t reserve capacity or remove the queue.

results.title: Pantera Capital Partner Breaks Down Four Structural Opportunities in the Compute Market | BroadChain.info
highlights:
The inference industry chain is divided into three layers: new cloud service providers such as Nebius and CoreWeave constitute GPU sellers; ready-to-use layers such as Fireworks and Baseten are GPU buyers; application layers such as Cursor, Perplexity, and Rime are Token demand-side participants. Rules of thumb show that for every $100 spent on Token fees at the application layer, about $45 flows to the ready-to-use layer, $50 flows to new cloud service providers, and $5 flows to routing layers such as OpenRouter. NVIDIA plays the role of the "central bank" of the compute market, managing the GPU depreciation cycle by controlling the pace of product releases, promoting the financialization of compute power to improve utilization, and announcing support for GPUs of up to 25% of residual value, acting as lender of last resort.

 Jay Yu divides compute market products into four categories. The physical delivery layer includes SF Compute, Hyperbolic, Vast, Runpod, and Compute Exchange, with the most durable long-term moat, but it requires rating agencies similar to Moody's to certify GPU quality. The index layer includes Ornn, Silicon Data, Compute Desk, and Semianalysis. CME and ICE have announced cooperation, but the spread between indices and individual GPU market prices is significant, and they are squeezed by upstream and downstream players. Derivatives trading platforms such as Liquid Compute and Architect provide cash-settled futures, but current trading volume is limited, with participants mainly OTC platforms and brokers. The financialization tools layer covers lending protocols, Vaults, and synthetic stablecoins such as USD.AI, providing support for financing data centers and new cloud service providers.

results.title: Pantera Capital: The Rise of the Computing Power Capital Market
results.author: JinseFinance 2026/09/10
highlights:
Currently, the financialization of GPU computing power is still in its early stages. Like electricity, computing power is not a completely homogeneous and interchangeable asset; it is subject to constraints based on SKU, time, and geographical location. However, looking ahead 5-10 years, computing power is very likely to evolve into a commodity asset like electricity and crude oil, becoming a key global resource supporting economic output in the AI ​​era. ... From a physical perspective, the electricity market essentially follows a three-tiered architecture of "grid, operator, and node." The top layer consists of multiple physically independent regional grids. Each regional grid has a system operator—a Regional Transmission Organization (RTO) and an Independent System Operator (ISO). Operators manage numerous local substation nodes. Taking San Francisco as an example, the city's power supply is jointly guaranteed by multiple substation "nodes" such as Embarcadero, Larkin, and Mission. The electricity price at each node is calculated using the Node Marginal Price (LMP) algorithm, which performs optimization under multiple constraints, including generation dispatch, user demand, transmission physical costs, and the physical laws of power flow. ... 1.2 Some Hypotheses about the Computing Power Market Looking back at the evolution of the electricity market over the past 30 years, we can deduce several hypotheses about the computing power market. ... Just as the electricity market has independent physical power grids, the computing power market will be divided according to hardware chip types. Different chip categories such as H100, H200, B200, and B300 each have independent (but interconnected) pricing benchmarks. At the "operator" level, there are multiple computing power service providers, such as AWS, Nebius, Coreweave, SF Compute, and Ornn. They set differentiated pricing for different clusters, which are distinguished by time, geographical location, and hardware model (SKU), corresponding to nodes in the electricity market. The closest corresponding mechanism to LMP is the scheduling/routing algorithm: outputting dynamic instance prices based on the resource availability of specific hardware specifications. ... In the future, a large number of benchmark indices will emerge in the computing power field, and those that ultimately win will most likely be those tied to highly liquid physical delivery venues. Furthermore, in the electricity market, although trading entities (power generators are short sellers, and load customers are long sellers) sometimes hedge directly on the electricity exchange, most transactions are completed through over-the-counter trading desks under banks and dealers. Over-the-counter (OTC) exchanges convert node delivery into hub delivery using a fixed price difference, thus hedging their own risk exposure. This market structure may also reappear in the computing power market: the actual trading entities of computing power (new cloud vendors and AI companies) may prefer to purchase corresponding hardware resources through brokers rather than directly hedging on exchanges. Finally, the basis risk in the computing power market may be significantly higher than in the electricity market. The Federal Electricity Act requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to mandate the disclosure of wholesale electricity prices, but the computing power market does not have such mandatory transparency requirements. This means that dynamic prices (and indices) for computing power can only be constructed based on their own order books, as well as the order books of new cloud vendors that cooperate through revenue sharing and data procurement agreements.

...

One possible evolutionary path for the computing power market is as follows: two types of AI trading entities—long-side (developer platforms, application layers) and short-side (new cloud vendors)—complete transactions of specific hardware specifications (SKUs) through computing power brokers such as SF Compute, Runpod, and Compute Exchange, and over-the-counter trading desks. The computing power brokers and over-the-counter desks then manage inventory and bear the basis risk between the hardware specifications required by end-to-end token consumers and the standard H200 computing power; they conduct hedging operations on computing power exchanges such as Architect and Pluto. The pricing of the exchanges relies on a benchmark price formed by weighted calculation of the order books of cooperating new cloud vendors and over-the-counter platforms.

...

However, even today, a significant price difference still exists between numerous computing power indices and various independent GPU trading markets. There are two main reasons for this price divergence: First, the underlying assets themselves differ, with different platforms varying greatly in terms of computing power reliability, interruptibility, and contract terms; second, the order book data relied upon by various computing power indices differs, and the computing power industry, unlike assets such as electricity (regulated by FERC), lacks mandatory information transparency regulations. Currently, many computing power indices simply purchase order book data in bulk from new cloud vendors or build their basic datasets through cooperation or revenue sharing. In addition, compared to exchanges and physical delivery businesses, the index layer itself is more difficult to commercialize. Therefore, although indices can generate momentum and are an indispensable part of the computing power market system, relying solely on index business will subject it to pressure from both the underlying physical market (price data source) and the upper-level exchanges (which demand revenue sharing). Product Three: Derivatives Trading Platform. The third layer of the technology stack is the trading platform (mainly cash-settled futures), which provides a hedging venue for computing power based on index products. Projects such as Liquid Compute and Architect are currently developing related projects. In the long term, the derivatives track is the most watched and has the strongest commercial potential, but it is still in its early stages, and the trading volume is not yet considerable. Furthermore, the tradable assets of the cash-settled platform are standardized H200 computing power instances, not specific hardware specifications that can directly run inference tasks. Therefore, most of the transactions conducted on these exchanges are conducted by over-the-counter trading desks and computing power brokers, aiming to hedge the risk of computing power inventory on their balance sheets, rather than the main consumers of end-user AI. Product Four: Financialization Vehicles. The fourth category of products has a broader scope, referring to various tools that facilitate computing power financing. Examples include lending agreements, fund pools, and synthetic stablecoins like USD.AI, providing financial support for the physical construction of data centers and new cloud vendors. In the future, the market will also see risk transfer and insurance products to smooth the basis risk in the GPU market. In summary, the outline of the final mature form of the computing power industry is clear: the winners will be full-stack players who can achieve stable physical GPU delivery, naturally generate computing power indices based on their own physical order books, and then build futures exchanges based on these indices, transforming computing power into an asset class that can hedge risks. The industry still has a point of contention regarding the order of product launches – will the ultimate winner prioritize physical delivery, the launch of an index, or the establishment of a trading platform? 3.2 Frontier Exploration of Computational Power Token Economics So far, the discussion has mainly focused on the GPU level of the computing power market. We will broaden our perspective and examine the computing power market from a broader perspective of computing power token economics, analyzing it from the angles of historical evolution, value capture, and game theory in its interaction with cutting-edge AI labs. From a historical perspective, the computing power trading market is not a new concept. ... It is worth noting that many participants did not stop at the GPU trading market level. For example, Hyperbolic transformed into an inference service provider, directly selling inference tokens; SF Compute began building its own clusters and operating its own computing resources. From a value distribution chain perspective, value is passed down layer by layer along the path: AI applications (Cursor, Harvey, Granola) → routing layers like OpenRouter → inference service providers like Fireworks and Baseten → new cloud vendors and computing power trading markets (Nebius, Coreweave, SF Compute) → data center operators. Holding a position in the middle of the industry chain makes one vulnerable to pressure from both ends; companies must extend their business upstream or downstream to maintain stable and substantial profit margins. Finally, from a game theory perspective, there are three core variables in the Token market that cannot be ignored: (1) Nvidia controls chip supply and depreciation pace; (2) cutting-edge labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI release new models, pushing up the demand for inference tokens; (3) open-source models such as Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, and Tongyi Qianwen continue to suppress the profit margin of inference business. These three variables together constitute the structural driving factors on both the bullish and bearish sides of the GPU and Token markets. The launch of a major product by either side can reshape the entire pricing curve. This is because major events (such as the release of GPT 5.6) will have a chain reaction along the entire AI Token value chain, causing drastic fluctuations in Token prices and physical GPU prices. It can be seen that it is highly economically reasonable for a company to operate both the inference token business and the physical GPU trading market at the same time, which can hedge against the risks brought about by the fluctuations in profit margins at both the upstream and downstream of the industry chain. Conclusion Looking back at history, the initial stages of large commodity markets such as crude oil and electricity are remarkably similar to the current computing power market: transactions relied on intermediaries for bilateral, opaque over-the-counter trading. Subsequently, physical delivery gradually evolved into standardized protocols and financial infrastructure components, including indices, standardized trading, and quality verification mechanisms, ultimately developing into a fully financialized asset class. The computing power industry is now replicating this evolution. Various projects have begun experimenting with financial instruments such as indices, cash-settled exchanges, lending, and insurance; simultaneously, GPU physical trading platforms and cloud service providers are making efforts to capture the entire token value chain. As the underlying asset supporting the entire AI economy, computing power is gradually transforming from simple infrastructure into an independent financial asset. The future of this sector will likely see the emergence of multiple unicorn companies, distributed across different levels of the industry chain, with diverse business models covering areas such as physical computing power supply, brokerage, lending, and risk management, while simultaneously being compatible with both decentralized finance (DeFi) and traditional finance (TradFi) capital markets. Computing power may be the first entirely new physical commodity to emerge in decades; we are witnessing it evolve from fragmented community trading into a mature and complete asset class.

highlights:
Observing electricity’s development allows speculation about computing power’s evolution. It may form a structure similar to that of the electricity market. Like electricity, computing power has heterogeneity, temporal attributes, and hub attributes, important for global economic growth. Physical delivery structures may be “hardware, suppliers, clusters.” Independent markets may form based on different hardware categories like H100, H200, B200, and B300, each with their own price benchmarks. Computing power suppliers such as AWS, Nebius, CoreWeave, SF Compute, and Ornn will provide different pricing mechanisms for specific clusters influenced by time, location, and SKU, similar to electricity nodes.

A scheduling or routing algorithm may dynamically generate computing power instance prices based on GPU availability. Benchmarks connected to high-liquidity physical delivery locations may become industry reference prices. Like in the electricity market where generators sometimes hedge in exchanges but most transactions are completed through over-the-counter (OTC) trading departments operated by banks, a similar structure may appear in the computing power market. AI companies and new cloud service providers may prefer to procure specific SKUs through brokers rather than directly hedging on exchanges.

...

The Token economic structure of participants will influence how the computing power capital market forms. Demand-side developer platforms and application layers, along with supply-side new cloud service providers, may trade specific SKUs through brokers and OTC platforms like SF Compute, Runpod, and Compute Exchange. Computing power brokers manage inventory and bear basis risk between end Token consumer requirements and general H200s. They can hedge through platforms like Architect or Pluto. Prices on these trading platforms are based on a computing power benchmark calculated as a weighted average of order book prices from new cloud service providers and collaborating OTC platforms.

results.title: What Needs to Happen for Compute Derivatives to Exist
results.author: Dave Friedman
highlights:
Suppose a compute provider signs a customer agreement for one million GPU-hours next quarter at $3 an hour. It expects to buy the capacity for $2 an hour, leaving $1 million before its other costs. Sales has secured the customer, procurement has found a supplier, and the deal looks profitable. The customer price, however, is fixed. The purchase price floats. If the supplier’s rate rises to $2.60, the expected contribution falls to $400,000. A 30% increase in input cost has removed 60% of the contribution, with everything else unchanged 1.

...

The provider earns the difference between what the customer pays and what the capacity costs. Because that difference is smaller than either price, a change in the purchase cost produces a larger percentage change in the amount left over.

The two percentages use different starting amounts:

- Input cost rises 30%: the $0.60 increase divided by the original $2.00 cost equals 30%.
- Contribution falls 60%: the same $0.60 increase eats into the original $1.000 spread. That leaves $0.40, a 60% reduction.

Every additional dollar paid to the supplier comes directly out of the amount left over, because customer revenue is fixed.

“Contribution” here means revenue minus the purchased capacity cost, before the proivder pays its other expenses. It is not net profit. If those other expenses were $500,000 in both cases, the provider would go from a $500,000 profit to a $100,000 loss.

That is the point of the example: a seemingly manageable change in compute prices can have a much larger effect on profitability when the provider operates on a relatively narrow spread.
